title: The afternoon slump
hook: the desert monks called it the noonday devil
tomorrow: what do you do at your own front door before walking in?

segments.voice: Yesterday, noon: a fixed minute and pray without ceasing, held together. The line was the noon pause.

The coffee's worn off. The email's been read and not answered. The window suddenly looks interesting, and so does the fridge, and so does anything happening in any other room. A monk in the Egyptian desert, long ago, knew this hour so well that he gave it a name from a psalm: the noonday demon. Not because he thought tired people were possessed. Because the pull felt like a voice, and a voice can be answered.
screen: `THE COFFEE'S WORN OFF.` → `THE WINDOW LOOKS INTERESTING.` → `A NAME FROM A PSALM.`

segments.voice: The monk was Evagrius, and the thing he named was acedia. Listen to how physical he makes it. The sun seems to stand still. The day feels endless. The monk keeps going to the window, watching for a visitor. His small cell starts to look hateful, and so does his work, and so do the brothers he lives with, and a thought whispers that he'd be holier somewhere else. In the Douay-Rheims, Psalm 90 promises protection from "the noonday devil." Bibles translated from the Hebrew read that line differently, but the desert monks prayed it this way. The Catechism still names acedia among the temptations of prayer. The desert's answer was plain: stay. Don't run from the cell; keep at the work. And John Cassian, who carried the desert teaching west, passed on one short psalm line for moments like this: "O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me." Here's the thing to tell a friend: that same line still opens the hours of the Church's daily prayer, said by people in monasteries and parishes. And Evagrius made a promise: whoever outlasts this demon comes through into a deep peace.
screen: `THE SUN STANDS STILL.` · `YOU'D BE HOLIER SOMEWHERE ELSE.` · `THE ANSWER: STAY.` · `O GOD, COME TO MY ASSISTANCE.` · then, large: `THE NOONDAY DEVIL.`

segments.voice: Stand and walk slowly for about a minute, feeling each foot land, the way a monk might pace a small cell without leaving it. Going one way, say the first half of Cassian's line, O God, come to my assistance; coming back, the second, O Lord, make haste to help me. Then sit down where you started, and stay. That staying is the whole desert teaching in one move.
The afternoon slump. The heavy, restless middle of the day, which the desert monks named acedia and learned to outlast.
Pocket this one: the noonday devil, easier to outlast once it has a name. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: 3 p.m. shift after school, trays piled up, and i want to quit right now. does that mean wrong job?
options: Not necessarily. Desert monks named that pull acedia, and their advice was to stay and outlast it.
Probably. A restless feeling like that is a sign you'd be better off somewhere else entirely.
No, but feel guilty about it. The monks taught that being tired is itself a kind of sin.
chat.meaning: Evagrius said acedia whispers you'd be better somewhere else. The desert answer was to stay put, keep working, and pray a short line.

Evagrius, Praktikos 12, paraphrased: the demon of acedia, also called the noonday demon; the sun seems to stand still, the day seems long, the monk looks out the window for visitors, hates his place, work and brothers, thinks of going elsewhere; the one who outlasts it reaches deep peace. Confirm.
'Bibles translated from the Hebrew read that line differently' (e.g. KJV Psalm 91:6 'the destruction that wasteth at noonday'); kept vague on purpose. Confirm.
Cassian's recommendation of Psalm 69:2 is in Conferences 10 (Abba Isaac); confirm section. 'Carried the desert teaching west': general description.
CCC 2733 names acedia among temptations in prayer; confirm. 'Still opens the hours of the Church's daily prayer': the Liturgy of the Hours' opening verse (Deus in adiutorium); confirm.
